passage.text: Pete urged his pony, Ranger, onward. After a long, hot day on the dusty trail, he was looking forward to a soft bed tonight at the station. Bobcat Kid, the next Pony Express rider, was waiting to carry the mail on to California.

Pete had signed up to ride for the new Pony Express in April 1860. Almost a year later, he still loved his adventures in the West. It was important work, bringing mail and news to people from far away. He'd never lost a letter.
Pete and Ranger reached the last hill before the station. On their left lay the open plain. To their right, the trail dropped off into a rocky path down to the river.
Ranger slowed his pace. Was something wrong? Pete looked around.

A cloud hung off to the left, low in the sky. Pete heard a rumble like thunder. But this wasn't a thunderstorm. The cloud got larger and closer. Pete saw dark heads, horns, and pounding feet. A herd of buffalo was heading straight for them.
Pete thought fast. He jumped down and grabbed the pony's reins. "Down the hill!" he shouted, pulling. The pony stood still. The ground shook with the pounding of hundreds of pairs of hooves.

Just before the buffalo reached them, Pete pulled Ranger safely off the trail. But as he dove down the steep bank, his shoulder slammed into a sharp rock. His mailbag tore open. While the herd roared along the trail above them, Pete watched one of his letters float away.

The thunder faded as the herd disappeared into the distance. Pete's letter settled into the branches of a bush on the hillside far below. Pete thought about that soft bed waiting at the station. He started leading Ranger back up to the trail. Nobody would miss just one little letter.

But Ranger wouldn't budge. Pete sighed. "You're right," he told his pony. Tying Ranger under a tree, Pete headed downhill. He slipped, and branches scratched his arms and his face. When he got to the bush, the letter was just out of reach. He jumped up to grab it. Once, twice, three times. Yes! He caught it. He climbed back up to Ranger, waving the letter. It was addressed to "Miss Emma Hunter."
"Let's go, Ranger," said Pete. "Miss Hunter will get her mail, and we've earned our beds tonight!"

passage.text: Jason, what are you bringing in for Spanish class tomorrow? asked Akash. Akash's sister Dhara caught up with them as they left the school.
"I have no idea," answered Jason. "It's too hard to think of anything."

Each week, they had to bring an object that started with a certain letter. They had to share some interesting facts about it. It all had to be in Spanish. Didn't Mr. Bermudez know they had only just started learning Spanish? It was impossible.
This week, their letter was c.
Jason couldn't think of a single Spanish word starting with c. The only thing he could do in Spanish was sing. Jason started humming "A Mi Burro." It was a song about a little donkey.
Dhara asked Jason why he looked mad. He rolled his eyes. "I'm not mad. I just can't think of a word that starts with c."
"Silly," she said. "I know something that starts with c."
But before Jason could say anything, she yelled, "Chocolate!"
Jason stared. "Yeah!" he said. "I even know the Spanish for that. Chocolate. Same spelling, different pronunciation!"

The next morning, Jason brought a big chocolate bar to school. But he'd skipped breakfast, so he was hungry. He peeled off the wrapper and took a quick bite to get him through math. He could bring half a chocolate bar to Spanish, right? It was still chocolate. One more bite would be fine. But before he knew it, Jason had eaten the whole bar. He had none left to show the class.
Before long, it was time for Spanish. He had a funny feeling in his stomach that had nothing to do with all of the chocolate.

Starting at the front of the classroom, the students got up to share their objects. Akash showed off his calcetines (socks). Hadi held up a corbata (necktie). Jason's turn was coming next. He couldn't sit still. He started humming "A Mi Burro." Suddenly he grinned.
Mr. Bermudez said, "Jason, it's your turn. What do you have?"
Jason stood up. He was ready. "Canción," he said. That was Spanish for "song." And he sang "A Mi Burro," with gusto, for the class. Then he took a bow.

passage.text: Most of the other sheep on the farm liked to do nothing but chew and talk. But Irma was bored. She needed a hobby!
Irma considered her options. Playing checkers? Checkers required two players. Irma asked Wilma if she wanted to learn. Wilma did not. Checkers was out.
Collecting stamps? Irma asked Velma if she knew how to collect stamps. Velma said it was too difficult to buy stamps at the post office. Stamp collecting was out.
"Sheep don't have hobbies," Velma and Wilma said.
"I'm different," Irma said.

Maybe she could try knitting. Just yesterday, she'd heard Farmer Max talking about learning to knit himself. Irma peeked through the farmhouse window. Farmer Max was sitting by the fire with knitting needles and a big tangle of yarn. He didn't look happy. He seemed to be trying to knit a bulky sweater. Irma watched carefully. She admired the bright purple yarn.

Irma daydreamed for a moment about knitting herself a beautiful purple sweater. When she looked up again, Farmer Max was outside. He stomped over to the garbage can, carrying the sweater. He pulled a loose end of purple yarn, and the sweater unraveled before Irma's eyes. Row after row of crooked stitches came undone. All that remained was a loose pile of yarn. Farmer Max dumped it all into the garbage. He threw his knitting needles into the garbage after the yarn. He tossed a sheet of sweater-knitting instructions on top of that. Then he trudged back to the house.
"Hrmmpph," Irma heard Farmer Max say. "A sheep could knit a better sweater than that!"
"Well," thought Irma, "maybe he's right." Carefully, she lifted Farmer Max's yarn, needles, and instructions out of the trash bin.
Wilma and Velma laughed. "Sheep don't knit," they said.

"I'm different," Irma said. Her first attempt failed, but she pulled out the stitches and tried again. And kept trying. She was happy. She loved the rich color of the purple yarn. Slowly, a sweater started taking shape.

Then one morning, Farmer Max announced to the sheep, "Shearing today!" A truck pulled up, and three men jumped down with their shears. They waded into the sheep pen. Quickly, one by one, they sheared each sheep, collected the wool, and let the sheep go.
That night the sheep huddled, complaining about their new haircuts.
Velma grumbled, "I'm cold!"
"Too windy for me!" whined Wilma.
"Not me," said Irma, wearing her lovely purple sweater. "I feel just right!"

"Sheep don't have hobbies," Velma and Wilma said.
"I'm different," Irma said.

She admired the bright purple yarn.

"Hrmmpph," Irma heard Farmer Max say. "A sheep could knit a better sweater than that!"
"Well," thought Irma, "maybe he's right." Carefully, she lifted Farmer Max's yarn, needles, and instructions out of the trash bin.

Velma grumbled, "I'm cold!"

passage.text: Greta and Ami had planned to kayak in Bluefish Bay. The day was warm and sunny. But Ami was sick and couldn't go out. Greta's parents usually didn't let her paddle alone. Today, though, Dad said it looked pretty safe. She just had to bring a life jacket.

So Greta took off, enjoying the freedom of the solo trip in the bright sunshine. At first she didn't notice when a sudden strong wind blew. But waves rose and fell, almost tipping her out of her kayak. The water turned dark. The wind grew. Rain began to pour. Greta paddled harder.
The wind was blowing her toward a huge, sharp rock. Greta's arms were tired. She could barely keep paddling. The rock grew closer and closer.

Suddenly she saw it. A dolphin! It jumped out of the water. It seemed to be playing. Greta had heard stories of dolphins saving people in storms. She didn't believe them. Still, the dolphin did make her feel safer.

Now the dolphin stopped jumping. It swam ahead of the kayak. Right before Greta reached the rock, the dolphin pushed the kayak away from danger. Greta sighed with relief as the kayak slid by the sharp rock. But then she saw the dolphin was herding her into a narrow bay.

The bay was lined with cliffs. Now Greta was heading straight for a wall of rock. She saw nowhere to land, only steep rock walls. The wind was blowing her toward the wall. She was going to smash into the cliff!

But the dolphin turned sharply. Greta sucked in her breath and followed, fighting the wind. Now she saw where the dolphin was leading her. A small rocky beach lay just ahead. Greta paddled hard for a few final strokes.

With one last pull, Greta made it to the shore. The waves were pounding, but she pulled the kayak out of the water and plopped down onto the beach. Now she'd be safe until the storm passed and she could paddle home.

She remembered the dolphin. Looking back out to sea, she saw her friend jump into the air. It flipped, splashed, and disappeared. "Thank you!" Greta yelled, jumping up and down and waving. She hoped the dolphin had heard her.
Now she knew those old stories were true. Just wait till she told Ami!

The plot is the events that happen in a story, or what the characters do. The plot of a story is often told in the order that the events happen.
The problem is something that goes wrong for the characters, or something that needs to be fixed or changed. The problem, or conflict, in a story often causes the characters to take action.

passage.text: Greta and Ami had planned to kayak in Bluefish Bay. The day was warm and sunny. But Ami was sick and couldn't go out. Greta's parents usually didn't let her paddle alone. Today, though, Dad said it looked pretty safe. She just had to bring a life jacket.

So Greta took off, enjoying the freedom of the solo trip in the bright sunshine. At first she didn't notice when a sudden strong wind blew. But waves rose and fell, almost tipping her out of her kayak. The water turned dark. The wind grew. Rain began to pour. Greta paddled harder.
The wind was blowing her toward a huge, sharp rock. Greta's arms were tired. She could barely keep paddling. The rock grew closer and closer.

Suddenly she saw it. A dolphin! It jumped out of the water. It seemed to be playing. Greta had heard stories of dolphins saving people in storms. She didn't believe them. Still, the dolphin did make her feel safer.

Now the dolphin stopped jumping. It swam ahead of the kayak. Right before Greta reached the rock, the dolphin pushed the kayak away from danger. Greta sighed with relief as the kayak slid by the sharp rock. But then she saw the dolphin was herding her into a narrow bay.

The bay was lined with cliffs. Now Greta was heading straight for a wall of rock. She saw nowhere to land, only steep rock walls. The wind was blowing her toward the wall. She was going to smash into the cliff!

But the dolphin turned sharply. Greta sucked in her breath and followed, fighting the wind. Now she saw where the dolphin was leading her. A small rocky beach lay just ahead. Greta paddled hard for a few final strokes.

With one last pull, Greta made it to the shore. The waves were pounding, but she pulled the kayak out of the water and plopped down onto the beach. Now she'd be safe until the storm passed and she could paddle home.

She remembered the dolphin. Looking back out to sea, she saw her friend jump into the air. It flipped, splashed, and disappeared. "Thank you!" Greta yelled, jumping up and down and waving. She hoped the dolphin had heard her.
Now she knew those old stories were true. Just wait till she told Ami!
